counting_rule: one materially distinct situation-action-result-validation unit; filenames and taxonomy combinations excluded
research_stop_rule: three discovery/deduplication loops over the declared authoritative source set; stop when a loop yields zero new admissible unique cases
source_binding_rule: SHA-256 over canonical URL, source locator, and evidence statement

cases.title: Carer's Allowance smart answers confused less-experienced users
cases.situation: Section-local answer summaries looked interactive and behaved inconsistently across page structures.
cases.action: Researchers observed where users misunderstood or became stuck.
cases.result: The feature did not meet the assumed need and created confusion.
cases.lesson: Do not add review/navigation affordances unless their scope and interaction are consistent with the user's mental model.
cases.validation: Observed user-research findings and subsequent live-service experiment.
cases.evidence: Users confused smart answers with new questions or controls; removing them did not change completion, time, claims, timeouts, or back-button behaviour.

cases.title: Feature removal was tested with before-and-after service metrics
cases.situation: The team did not know whether removing smart answers would harm completion.
cases.action: They compared completion rate, completion time, claims, timeouts, and behaviour before and after removal.
cases.result: No material degradation was observed.
cases.lesson: Removal is a testable design intervention; validate it with a stated hypothesis and multiple guardrail metrics.
cases.validation: Live-service before/after measurement.
cases.evidence: Completion rates, average completion time and claims stayed stable after removal, with no increase in timeouts.

cases.title: End-of-application check answers matched the user mental model
cases.situation: Users expected to review the whole application rather than section-local summaries.
cases.action: The team prototyped a final check-and-change answers page.
cases.result: User feedback consistently supported the revised pattern.
cases.lesson: Place review at the natural commitment boundary and allow correction before submission.
cases.validation: Prototype testing plus satisfaction-survey feedback.
cases.evidence: Users expected final review; the check-answers prototype met that need and was supported by survey feedback.

cases.title: Optional education fields obscured what was actually required
cases.situation: A form presented many optional fields without a clear information hierarchy.
cases.action: Researchers tested a single-page version without optional fields.
cases.result: Users understood and completed the section faster.
cases.lesson: Optional questions are not free: each adds interpretation and decision cost.
cases.validation: Comparative prototype test.
cases.evidence: Optional fields caused uncertainty; a coherent single page without them was clearer and faster.

cases.title: Fewer, coherently grouped education questions improved speed and data quality
cases.situation: The education section was slow and confusing.
cases.action: Questions were regrouped and optional fields removed or made explicitly mandatory.
cases.result: Average completion time fell and submitted information became more complete and faster to process.
cases.lesson: A smaller, explicit question set can improve both user effort and downstream operational quality.
cases.validation: Live completion-time and processing-quality data.
cases.evidence: Completion times decreased; information became more complete and faster to process.

cases.title: Reordering employment questions did not remove the underlying burden
cases.situation: Employment questions added about 14 minutes and required hard-to-retrieve dates and payslips.
cases.action: The team reordered questions and reduced page count.
cases.result: Completion time stayed the same; only the number of steps decreased slightly.
cases.lesson: Flow polish cannot compensate for an intrinsically burdensome information demand.
cases.validation: Live completion-time comparison.
cases.evidence: The redesign made the section clearer but did not improve time because dates and payslip demands remained.

cases.title: Reduce hard-to-recall employment data rather than merely rearranging it
cases.situation: A presentational redesign failed to reduce completion time.
cases.action: The team moved to remove optional fields, clarify mandatory fields, ask for fewer old dates, and review employer contact and payslip requests.
cases.result: The improvement plan attacked policy and evidence burden rather than surface layout.
cases.lesson: Escalate unresolved UX friction to policy, data, and operational-process redesign.
cases.validation: Re-test completion time, abandonment, data completeness, and manual follow-up after implementation.
cases.evidence: The team identified underlying evidence demands and planned to remove or change them.

cases.title: Hidden support and the wrong phone destination created avoidable handoffs
cases.situation: A helpline was behind a disclosure and pointed to technical support although users needed eligibility help.
cases.action: The number was made prominent and call behaviour observed.
cases.result: Calls were transferred because the support destination did not match the user need.
cases.lesson: Support discoverability and support routing must be designed as one end-to-end service.
cases.validation: Call-routing observations and satisfaction feedback.
cases.evidence: Users struggled to find the number and most calls were transferred from technical support to the benefit unit.

cases.title: Contextual help did not automatically improve completion
cases.situation: The team introduced contextual links and a help guide.
cases.action: They monitored completion after the change.
cases.result: Early data did not show an increased completion rate.
cases.lesson: Do not equate shipping help content with a successful outcome; retain an inconclusive or failed result until metrics improve.
cases.validation: Post-release completion-rate monitoring.
cases.evidence: The published update said the help guide had not increased completion rates so far.

cases.title: Give ineligible users an explicit safe exit
cases.situation: Users told they might not be entitled could only continue into a lengthy application.
cases.action: The team improved eligibility signposting and created a route back to GOV.UK.
cases.result: The flow better represented a legitimate non-completion outcome.
cases.lesson: A good service distinguishes successful completion from a correct early exit.
cases.validation: Measure reason-coded exits separately from harmful abandonment.
cases.evidence: The original message forced users onward; the update added clearer signposting and an exit route.

cases.title: A non-navigable progress indicator created false affordance and anxiety
cases.situation: Users either did not notice the indicator or expected it to support navigation; some were intimidated by the section count.
cases.action: Researchers tested removal.
cases.result: Completion and time were unchanged.
cases.lesson: Progress UI must answer a demonstrated question and match expected interaction.
cases.validation: User observation and live-service removal experiment.
cases.evidence: Users missed or misread the indicator; removal did not reduce completion.

cases.title: Removing an unhelpful progress component preserved outcomes
cases.situation: A progress component consumed attention without meeting the user need.
cases.action: The component was removed and key service metrics monitored.
cases.result: Completion and average time stayed stable while claims rose slightly, not significantly.
cases.lesson: A simpler system with fewer misleading components can be a successful design outcome.
cases.validation: Live guardrail metrics and follow-up feedback.
cases.evidence: Removing the indicator caused no loss in completion or time and clarified the actual need for coarse progress information.

cases.title: Touch-screen continuous throttles removed tactile state feedback
cases.situation: Ship thrust was controlled through touch-screen throttles that could be independently ganged or unganged.
cases.action: NTSB analysed the interface, transfer sequence, operator actions, and standards.
cases.result: The interface increased the likelihood of operator errors contributing to a fatal collision.
cases.lesson: Safety-critical continuous controls require immediate, perceivable state and mode feedback; visual-only controls may be inadequate.
cases.validation: Independent accident reconstruction, logs, interviews, and standards comparison.
cases.evidence: NTSB found unnecessary transfer complexity and loss of tactile feedback increased operator-error likelihood.

cases.title: Unilateral steering-control transfer made a hidden mode change possible
cases.situation: In backup manual mode another station could take steering without acknowledgement.
cases.action: Investigators reconstructed control transfer from video and steering logs.
cases.result: Control and mode changed in less than a second while operators perceived a system malfunction.
cases.lesson: Transfer of authority must be explicit, acknowledged, visible to all affected operators, and reversible.
cases.validation: Video and steering-log correlation.
cases.evidence: The system allowed unilateral transfer and mode change, increasing the potential for the observed error.

cases.title: Use physical continuous controls and conspicuous mode indication for critical steering
cases.situation: Touch controls provided less direction, force, and gang-state feedback than mechanical throttles.
cases.action: NTSB recommended human-engineering standards be incorporated into modernization.
cases.result: The corrective design direction restores multimodal feedback and reduces ambiguous control state.
cases.lesson: Match the control modality to the physical continuity, risk, and feedback needs of the task.
cases.validation: Conformance to ASTM F1166 plus representative bridge simulation.
cases.evidence: NTSB contrasted tactile mechanical throttles with touch controls and recommended applying human-engineering design principles.

cases.title: Bind interface modes to operating procedures and demonstrated proficiency
cases.situation: Written procedures omitted transfer and ganging steps, and training had no standard for them.
cases.action: NTSB recommended revised procedures and proficiency requirements.
cases.result: The improvement closes the gap between interface capability, operating instructions, and operator competence.
cases.lesson: A UI is not operationally complete until procedures and training cover normal, transfer, exception, and recovery states.
cases.validation: Procedure traceability and observed proficiency tests.
cases.evidence: NTSB found procedures and training inadequate and required transfer operations to be explicitly taught and demonstrated.

cases.title: EHR interface use errors can become patient-safety events
cases.situation: Poorly written messages, colour misuse, missing information, truncated drug names, and inconsistent patient data can induce wrong actions.
cases.action: NIST synthesized incident evidence and interface reviews.
cases.result: Usability defects were treated as predictable safety risks rather than user blame.
cases.lesson: Risk assessment must include design-induced acts and omissions, especially for irreversible or harmful tasks.
cases.validation: Clinical and human-factors expert review against representative safety scenarios.
cases.source_locator: executive summary and EUP expert-review examples
cases.evidence: NIST identifies design-induced use error and examples including truncated drug names and incomplete allergy information.

cases.title: EHR safety validation uses application analysis, expert review, and user testing
cases.situation: A single heuristic review cannot prove safe performance.
cases.action: NIST defined a three-step EUP: application analysis, independent expert review, and representative-user validation testing.
cases.result: Critical tasks are tied to measurable completion, errors, corrected errors, sequence failures, and post-test risk interviews.
cases.lesson: Validation needs layered methods and performance evidence, not checklist-only approval.
cases.validation: The published EUP protocol itself specifies the independent validation method.
cases.evidence: NIST requires application analysis, expert review, and qualified usability testing of realistic critical tasks.

cases.title: Triangulate critical-use risks across observations, interviews, tests, and expert reviews
cases.situation: Safety risks vary by user, setting, product, and workflow.
cases.action: NIST used surveys, two-site observations, 40 interviews, usability tests on five EHRs, and expert reviews.
cases.result: The multi-method evidence supported empirically based critical-use cases.
cases.lesson: High-risk UX claims need converging evidence from multiple user types and methods.
cases.validation: Method and sample provenance documented by NIST.
cases.evidence: NIST documents five data methods, two health systems, 40 interviews, five EHR usability tests, and expert reviews.

cases.title: Workflow mismatch drives unsafe and inefficient EHR workarounds
cases.situation: EHR workflows did not adequately support clinical cognitive work and flexible task sequencing.
cases.action: Clinicians developed workarounds such as copying prior notes.
cases.result: Information quality, workload, and patient-safety risks increased.
cases.lesson: Workarounds are evidence of a system-work mismatch and should trigger root-cause analysis, not normalization.
cases.validation: Workflow observation, clinician discussions, and literature convergence.
cases.evidence: NIST reports workflow-integration challenges and frequent copy/paste workarounds.

cases.title: Model clinical workflow before choosing interface functions
cases.situation: Billing-centred EHR design conflicted with clinician-centred goals.
cases.action: NIST applied process mapping and goal-means decomposition with physicians and interdisciplinary experts.
cases.result: The study identified role views, task memory, workload balancing, copied-text distinction, referral tracking, and flexible sequencing opportunities.
cases.lesson: Derive functions from observed goals, coordination, variability, and workload rather than from database structure.
cases.validation: SME correction, interdisciplinary review, iterative diagrams, and published-evidence convergence.
cases.evidence: The workflow models generated concrete design opportunities and were iteratively reviewed by clinical and human-factors experts.

cases.title: NPS combined behavioural analytics with direct customer feedback
cases.situation: Analytics showed what visitors did but not why.
cases.action: NPS combined Digital Analytics Program data with GSA Touchpoints feedback.
cases.result: The team could target improvements using both behaviour and stated experience.
cases.lesson: Pair quantitative behaviour with qualitative explanation before prioritising UX changes.
cases.validation: Cross-source convergence and post-change metric monitoring.
cases.evidence: Digital.gov describes NPS integration of web analytics and customer feedback to target improvements.

cases.title: USA.gov tested accessibility with people using assistive technology
cases.situation: Conformance checks alone did not reveal lived navigation problems.
cases.action: The UX team studied blind and deaf participants using assistive technology.
cases.result: They identified carousel difficulty, mobile preference, and dependence on clear headings and action-oriented labels.
cases.lesson: Accessibility validation must include representative users and their actual assistive technologies.
cases.validation: Participant study with disability-community partnership.
cases.source_locator: Designing for people with disabilities case summary
cases.evidence: The federal case study reports observed assistive-technology habits and concrete navigation barriers.

cases.title: USAGov relaunch used human-centred evidence and continued iteration
cases.situation: USA.gov and USAGov en Español needed improved discoverability and task coverage.
cases.action: The team relaunched using human-centred design, then used usability tests, comments, click behaviour, and a task backlog.
cases.result: Visitor satisfaction and task accomplishment increased.
cases.lesson: Launch is a measurement point; sustained success requires an evidence-backed improvement backlog.
cases.validation: Usability tests, visitor feedback, click data, and outcome trends.
cases.source_locator: One year with the new USAGov case summary
cases.evidence: Digital.gov reports noticeable increases in visitor satisfaction and task accomplishment after evidence-led iteration.

cases.title: Website value should be measured as a multidimensional index
cases.situation: A single traffic or satisfaction metric could not represent website success.
cases.action: GSA developed a composite indicator spanning six components of website value.
cases.result: Teams gained a more balanced view of performance and trade-offs.
cases.lesson: Define success with multiple outcome dimensions and guardrails instead of optimising one convenient metric.
cases.validation: Composite-measure review and trend analysis.
cases.evidence: GSA describes compiling six website-success parameters into one indicator.

cases.title: Login.gov expanded language access through an explicit translation programme
cases.situation: English-only or ad-hoc translation limited access and created inconsistent support.
cases.action: Login.gov added languages through a documented translation approach.
cases.result: The public received expanded language access and assistance.
cases.lesson: Multilingual UX requires managed terminology, content governance, testing, and support—not literal string substitution.
cases.validation: Language-specific content review and representative-user task testing.
cases.evidence: Digital.gov documents Login.gov adding languages to expand public access and assistance.

cases.title: A shared government design system reduces repeated work while preserving accessibility
cases.situation: Service teams otherwise recreate common components and repeat solved accessibility work.
cases.action: GOV.UK maintains researched, reusable styles, components, patterns, and community contribution routes.
cases.result: Teams can build more consistent services from shared evidence and experience.
cases.lesson: Treat the design system as a governed product with research, accessibility, release notes, and contribution loops.
cases.validation: Component research, accessibility testing, versioned releases, and cross-service adoption evidence.
cases.source_locator: home page principles, components, community and accessibility sections
cases.evidence: The official system states that teams reuse accessible components and learn from other service teams' research and experience.

cases.title: Voting-system usability certification needs performance-based requirements
cases.situation: General or low-level design prescriptions did not reliably prevent voter errors or exclusion.
cases.action: NIST reviewed research, standards, guidelines, and evaluation methods and recommended performance-based usability requirements.
cases.result: The validation approach targets accuracy, spoiled-ballot reduction, disability access, and limited-English access.
cases.lesson: For civic and high-stakes systems, certify observable task performance across diverse users rather than visual conformance alone.
cases.validation: Qualification/certification testing against complete user-related functional requirements.
cases.evidence: NIST recommends performance-based standards and complete user-related functional requirements for voting products.

cases.title: Universal Credit was designed as an online, phone, and jobcentre service
cases.situation: Claimant needs and service operations cross digital and assisted channels.
cases.action: The service team treated the service as the total offer, including online, telephone, jobcentres, operations, and support.
cases.result: The design scope incorporated channel handoffs and operational support rather than only web screens.
cases.lesson: Model the full service and its support ecosystem before optimising a single interface.
cases.validation: End-to-end journey and operational-service assessment.
cases.evidence: The official case bank describes the service as a total offer across online, telephone, jobcentres, operations, and support.

cases.title: Safety-critical UI requires higher-fidelity workflow modelling and testing
cases.situation: Method selection can under-test complex or safety-critical work.
cases.action: NIST compared human-factors workflow methods and tied fidelity to system purpose and risk.
cases.result: Higher-risk systems are directed toward greater modelling fidelity and subsequent evaluation.
cases.lesson: Scale validation fidelity, scenario realism, and independence with consequence severity.
cases.validation: Risk-based selection of observation, walkthrough, simulation, expert review, and summative tests.
cases.evidence: NIST states that safety-critical systems require higher-fidelity modelling and greater subsequent validation.
